Newborn Care

Torticollis: a tilted neck in babies, children and adults

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Torticollis describes an unusual tilted or turned position of the head. It can be present early in a baby’s life or develop later after an illness, injury or movement disorder. Finding the cause is the first step: an infant with a tight neck muscle needs a different assessment and treatment plan from an adult with repeated involuntary neck spasms.

What torticollis means

The head often tips toward one shoulder while the chin points in the other direction, although the pattern can vary. Neck movement may be restricted, and pain or stiffness can occur. The term describes a posture or sign rather than one single disease.

Congenital means that the problem developed before or around birth; acquired means it appeared later. A temporary muscle spasm differs from a persistent structural restriction or a neurological movement disorder. The word acute refers to recent onset and does not mean permanent or fixed.

Some forms improve quickly, while others need ongoing care or can return. Early assessment is particularly helpful in babies because movement habits and head shape are developing. It is not possible to choose the right treatment just from the direction of the tilt.

Muscular torticollis in babies

Congenital muscular torticollis usually involves tightness or shortening of the sternocleidomastoid, or SCM, on one side of the neck. This muscle helps turn and bend the head. There may be a firm thickened area within it, but not every baby has a noticeable lump.

Positioning in the womb and muscle-related changes around birth may contribute; the exact mechanism is not always clear. A simple head preference can also occur without true muscle tightness. Neither situation should automatically be described as an inherited disease or proven damage to the neck’s blood supply.

Parents may notice that their baby looks mainly one way, has trouble turning toward a feed on one side or consistently rests on the same part of the head. Persistent asymmetry can accompany a flat area of the skull or uneven facial appearance.

Movement development should be checked as well. Some babies need help building balanced movement and opportunities for awake play. Hearing or eye problems are not inevitable effects of a tight SCM; unusual findings can point to a separate or underlying cause that needs assessment.

A new head tilt in an older child or adult

A neck may become stiff or tilted after an awkward sleeping position or muscle strain. Ear, throat or other nearby infections and swollen lymph nodes can also accompany a head tilt. Injury can affect muscles, joints, bones or nerves.

These possibilities should not all be grouped as harmless temporary torticollis. Fever, trouble swallowing, neurological changes or a significant injury can indicate a problem needing urgent investigation. Some medicines can trigger sudden dystonic reactions, and an eye-movement problem can sometimes alter head posture.

Uncomplicated muscular cases often improve over several days, sometimes around a week or longer. A promise that every episode will disappear in one or two days is not reliable. Persistent, recurrent or unexplained symptoms need follow-up.

A new tilt in a baby who previously moved normally also deserves a fresh assessment. Do not assume it is congenital muscular torticollis simply because the child is still young.

Structural causes and Klippel-Feil syndrome

A lasting restriction may arise from muscle contracture, scarring or differences in the neck bones. These causes are not interchangeable, and forcing the neck to move can be inappropriate when there is a structural problem.

Klippel-Feil syndrome is a rare condition in which two or more neck vertebrae are joined from birth. It can limit movement or cause a short-looking neck or head tilt. Some affected people also have hearing or eye differences, while others have relatively few signs.

Certain forms involve instability or pressure on the spinal cord or nerves. Specialist advice about activity and treatment is therefore important. This syndrome is distinct from the common infant problem of one tight neck muscle, even when the outward posture looks similar.

Cervical dystonia is a different condition

Cervical dystonia, also called spasmodic torticollis, is a neurological condition causing involuntary neck-muscle contractions. The head may twist or tilt sideways, forward or backward, sometimes with jerking or tremor. It can be painful and interfere with daily activities.

It is most often recognized in adults, especially in middle age, and is more common in women, but it is not limited to one sex or age bracket. Sometimes there is a family or other medical connection; often the precise cause is unknown, described as idiopathic.

Symptoms may occasionally ease without treatment and later return. The aim of care is usually to reduce involuntary movement, pain and disability. Adult dystonia treatments should not be applied to a baby with an ordinary positional preference.

Signs to notice and when to seek urgent help

Possible signs include difficulty turning the head, neck pain or stiffness, headaches, a raised shoulder, tight or prominent neck muscles and a chin that points away from the usual midline position. Symptoms can appear suddenly or develop gradually, depending on the cause.

Seek urgent assessment for a new head tilt after injury, or with fever, marked pain, drooling, difficulty swallowing, weakness, altered walking, unusual eye movements or a severe headache. Breathing difficulty or a child who is severely unwell requires emergency help.

Do not attempt a stretch or massage to test whether an injured or acutely painful neck will loosen. For a baby with a persistent preference but no emergency signs, arrange an early clinical review rather than waiting for a visible flat spot or developmental difficulty.

What happens at the appointment

The clinician will ask when the tilt began, whether it is constant, which movements are difficult and whether there has been illness, injury or a medication change. For a baby, feeding position, head shape, play and developmental progress are relevant.

Examination may include neck muscles and movement, the spine, eye movements and neurological function. A baby’s hips may also be assessed because hip dysplasia can be associated with congenital muscular torticollis.

Tests are selected for the findings. Typical congenital muscular torticollis does not routinely require neck imaging. An X-ray, ultrasound, MRI or other scan may help when the presentation is atypical or a bone, mass, infection or neurological cause is suspected.

Electromyography, or EMG, measures electrical muscle activity and may be useful in selected neurological assessments or treatment planning. It is not a routine test that every child with a head tilt needs. Ask what question a proposed test is intended to answer.

Early treatment and home care for babies

For confirmed muscular torticollis, early physiotherapy and caregiver teaching can improve neck movement and symmetry. The plan may combine gentle stretching, active movement, positioning and activities that encourage the baby to use both sides of the body.

Have a qualified clinician demonstrate exactly how to support your baby and which direction to move. Side bending and rotation are different movements; a vague instruction to stretch toward the affected side can be misleading. Do not force a movement or continue through obvious pain or distress.

A therapist may suggest changing where you sit, hold a toy or support the baby during feeding so that turning becomes part of ordinary interaction. The appropriate side depends on the examination. Keep feeding comfortable rather than making the baby struggle to reach the breast or bottle.

Offer short, frequent periods of supervised tummy play while the baby is awake, building up as tolerated and advised. This gives opportunities to strengthen the neck and shoulders. Vary awake positions and avoid using a car seat as a routine place for play outside travel.

Continue to put the baby on their back for sleep in a clear, firm, flat sleep space. Tummy time is for awake play. Do not use pillows, wedges or a positioning device to hold the neck during sleep.

Keep the agreed follow-up appointments so progress can be assessed. If the tilt, movement restriction or head shape is not improving, the diagnosis and treatment plan should be reviewed rather than simply stretching harder. There is no single home routine or fixed recovery deadline suitable for all babies.

Treatment for acquired torticollis and dystonia

Acquired torticollis is treated according to its cause. Once a simple muscle problem has been assessed, age-appropriate pain relief, guided activity and sometimes warmth or gentle massage may help. Infection, an injury or a medicine reaction requires a different approach.

Neck collars, traction or other supports are used only in selected circumstances under clinical supervision. They are not ordinary home treatment for every stiff neck. Forceful neck manipulation is not something to try on a baby or an unexplained painful neck.

For cervical dystonia, specialist injections of botulinum toxin can temporarily reduce overactive muscle contractions. Repeat treatment is commonly needed after a few months. The clinician balances benefit against effects such as weakness or swallowing difficulty.

Selected oral medicines may relax muscles or alter movement-related nerve signaling. Some drug classes are also used in other movement disorders, but this does not mean that any Parkinson’s medicine is suitable for torticollis. Physiotherapy and symptom-management strategies may form part of the plan.

When procedures or surgery are considered

Most babies with muscular torticollis do not need surgery. If significant restriction persists despite appropriate treatment, an orthopedic specialist may consider a procedure to release or lengthen the tight muscle. The decision depends on the diagnosis, severity and response to care.

A structural spinal problem may instead need treatment for instability, deformity or nerve compression, sometimes including a stabilization or fusion operation. An already fused vertebra is not, by itself, a reason to recommend another fusion.

For severe cervical dystonia that has not responded adequately to less invasive care, selected procedures include interrupting signals to particular muscles through nerve surgery or deep-brain stimulation. Deep-brain stimulation uses an implanted system to influence movement signals. These are specialist options for particular diagnoses, not routine treatments for infant torticollis.

Recovery and living with persistent symptoms

Many infant muscular cases improve with early, consistent care. Temporary muscle-related episodes in older people may settle, while structural or neurological causes can require longer-term management. Improvement and recurrence depend on the cause rather than the label alone.

Persistent pain or restricted movement can affect sleep, work, self-care, driving and social contact. Neurological symptoms from nerve or spinal compression need medical assessment; they should not simply be accepted as part of a sore neck.

People with chronic dystonia may feel isolated or low in mood. Tell the care team about those effects and ask about counseling, practical support or a local or online support group. Supportive contact can complement treatment, although it does not replace assessment of worsening symptoms.

For follow-up, note which activities are difficult, what has improved and any treatment side effects. In children, keep checking comfortable movement, head position and development as they grow. A useful plan explains both what to do now and when to seek another review.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Torticollis is a sign with several possible causes; infant muscular tightness and adult cervical dystonia require different care.

Early assessment and individually demonstrated physiotherapy are central to infant muscular treatment.

New torticollis with trauma, fever, swallowing difficulty or neurological changes needs prompt investigation.

Awake supervised tummy play does not change the recommendation for back sleeping.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record a head preference, feeding difficulties and questions for the clinician. It cannot determine the cause of a tilt or teach a safe hands-on neck stretch from a general description.

When to seek help

Seek urgent assessment for an injured, acutely painful or fever-associated tilted neck, or new neurological symptoms. Breathing difficulty or severe illness needs emergency help. Do not force the neck or use sleep positioners.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Have a persistent infant head preference assessed early.
  • A tilted neck does not always mean a tight muscle, and it is not always painful.
  • Learn the exact home plan from the baby’s physiotherapist; avoid generic side-specific stretch instructions.
  • Keep tummy time awake and supervised, with back sleeping for naps and nights.
  • Medicines, collars and surgery depend on a confirmed diagnosis.

Frequently asked questions

Is torticollis always painful?

No. Some babies mainly show a head preference or restricted movement. Acquired muscle spasm and cervical dystonia can be painful, sometimes substantially. New marked pain, fever or an injury needs assessment rather than being assumed to be ordinary infant tightness.

Will a baby with torticollis get better?

Many babies with congenital muscular torticollis improve with early physiotherapy and a correctly taught home plan. Recovery depends on the cause and severity. Surgery is uncommon and is considered only for selected persistent problems.

What causes a tilted neck?

Possible causes include infant muscle tightness, a postural preference, injury, infection, a bone difference, an eye problem or a neurological movement disorder. Some underlying conditions have genetic contributions, but torticollis as a sign is not automatically inherited.

What signs should I look for?

A head tilt or preference, reduced turning, neck stiffness, a raised shoulder or changes in head shape can be clues. In a baby, feeding on one side may be harder. Pain, fever, injury or new neurological symptoms change the urgency of assessment.

Which way should I stretch my baby’s neck?

Ask the physiotherapist to demonstrate the direction, support and amount of movement for your baby. Rotation and side bending are different, and the plan depends on which structures are restricted. Do not force a movement or use a generic instruction based only on the visible tilt.

Should my baby sleep on the tummy to correct the tilt?

No. Tummy play should happen only while awake and supervised. Place the baby on their back for sleep in a clear, firm, flat sleep space. Do not use pillows, wedges or devices to hold the head in position.

Does every child need an MRI or EMG?

No. Typical congenital muscular torticollis is often assessed clinically. Imaging or muscle-activity testing is selected when the history or examination suggests another cause or it would help specialist care.

Is cervical dystonia the same as infant muscular torticollis?

No. Cervical dystonia involves involuntary muscle contractions related to a movement disorder, usually recognized in adults. Infant muscular torticollis commonly involves tightness of one SCM muscle. Their treatments and expected course differ.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
